The grey gurnard Eutrigla gurnardus exhibits a life history strategy shaped by the cool waters of the northeastern Atlantic. Females deposit demersal eggs during an extended spawning season, and the resulting yolk-sac larvae rely on endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Under controlled incubation at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the duration from fertilisation to eclosion is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a relatively rapid developmental period consistent with other triglid species that spawn in shallow, seasonally warm coastal habitats. Neonates emerge as prolarvae measuring just over a millimetre in diameter from the yolk-dependent stage; the calculated wet weight at birth derived from an average egg diameter of 1.4 millimetres is 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], reflecting the modest maternal investment per offspring. This small initial size contrasts sharply with the substantial growth that occurs over the first few years of life, as individuals progress through planktonic larval and benthic juvenile stages before approaching their asymptotic dimensions.

Growth trajectories compiled from otolith readings indicate that female grey gurnard reach a total length at puberty of 18.8 centimetres [Lp = 18.8 centimetres]. Somatic growth is rapid during the first two years, after which the rate decelerates markedly as energy is increasingly channelled into gonad development. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, estimated from length–weight relationships derived from field-caught specimens, is approximately 37 grams [Wwp = approximately 37 grams]. This value represents a considerable increase over the neonatal mass, highlighting the intense feeding activity that characterises the juvenile phase, during which the fish prey on small crustaceans and juvenile fish. Achieving this body size is a prerequisite for the onset of vitellogenesis and the maturation of ovarian tissue, which typically commences during the winter months prior to the first spawning season. The length at which maturity is attained shows relatively low variability across the species range, suggesting a consistent size threshold that is modulated by local thermal regimes and food availability.

Adult females of Eutrigla gurnardus can attain an ultimate total length of 60 centimetres [Li = 60 centimetres], although individuals exceeding 50 centimetres are uncommon in most commercial catches. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females, derived from the species-specific length–weight conversion, reaches approximately 1,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,300 grams]. This asymptotic body size places the grey gurnard among the larger members of the Triglidae, a family characterised by robust, benthic-oriented body plans. The growth trajectory to this maximum size is protracted, with the oldest individuals in the population approaching the upper limits of the species lifespan. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have documented that the maximum lifespan in the wild, under the prevailing thermal conditions of the North Sea at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years]. This extended longevity, combined with iteroparous reproduction, allows females to accumulate multiple spawning opportunities across their lifetime, partially offsetting the relatively low mass-specific fecundity per event.

The reproductive output of female grey gurnard is tightly linked to body size and ambient temperature. Under the cool conditions typical of their core distribution at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the age at which females achieve first reproduction has been estimated at approximately 2.5 years after hatching [tR = approximately 2.5 years after hatching]. This delayed maturation relative to many small-bodied shelf fishes reflects the time required to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves for the first spawning event. Once mature, females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that integrates both batch fecundity and spawning frequency. Field observations indicate that at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], a single female can produce a clutch of roughly 822 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 822 eggs per spawning event], and that individuals typically complete one spawning event per day [F_R_i = one spawning event per day] during the peak of the season. The high daily output compensates for the relatively small egg size and consequently low per-offspring investment.
